If you come to Turkey and order "Turkish breakfast" anywhere, you'll get multiple kinds of cheese, olives and jams, simit (traditional Turkish bagel covered with sesame), honey with cream, butter, sucuk (traditional Turkish sausage with lots of spices), tomatos, cucumbers, maybe even kuymak (a dish that is made of cheese, butter and corn flour) AND a menemen. If there are full Engilsh or full Irısh breakfasts, there should be a full Turkish breakfast too. We also have tea with traditional Turkish breakfast and then have a Turkish coffee afterwards. In Turkish, we call breakfast "kahvaltı" which means before coffee and that's why you get Turkish coffee after.

Content:

Just finding British style sausages in the US is probably tricky, let alone good ones (or particularly and purposefully shit ones). Also, I've never seen bubble and squeak with a full breakfast, the toast needs to be less fancy and lathered in salted butter and HP brown sauce is like a requirement to have on hand and try. The condiment is so iconic in pairing that is practically an ingredient in itself.

But I'm actually gonna take a turn and say the English Breakfast, whilst good, is just a famous novelty. The king of British breakfasts is the Bacon Roll/Butty, with or without a runny fried egg. Or buttered crumpets.

Author: @EVLP1917
Content:
Few things about the pão de queijo/Brazilian breakfast: 

- Generally it would be a guava paste/jam called Goiabada. But it's not uncommon to see strawberry jam with it (Or grape or some other flavors for jam). 

- Pão de queijo also fits A FUCKTON with doce de leite (Dulce de leche). I'd recommend you try a doce de leite de Minas com café, which is a a dulce de leche with coffe notes and tones, I'm not much of a sweets kind of guy (More into savory/salty stuff) and that is the best thing ever, I'd eat it straight from the jar. 

- If you want a combination with something more savory/salt, I'd go with a (Very light) spread of salted butter or requeijão (Brazilian very soft serve cheese). 

- There are other ways of eating pão de queijo, and some of them it will include Brazilian calabresa (A type of sausage) grated in bits. 

- And finally, for the big reveal: this isn't definitely our "full breakfast". As you mentioned with India, there a lot of ways to eat breakfast here in Brazil. Sure, if you're late, you'd eat only the pão de queijo sometimes. But since other countries could be represented by a whole variety that you would only prepare when you have the time: pão na chapa (Bread with butter pressed on the pan), a pão na chapa com saída ou entrada requeijão (Explained what it is before, it will make the requeijão crisp up if it's entrada requeijão), some type of cake is also common (Cuca or bolo de fubá are also very breakfasty) and some cold cuts like presunto and queijo (Ham and cheese) for the pão francês to make misto quente or some peito de peru e queijo minas ou queijo branco, salame, hell, even a tapioca with light butter on it. If you have the time to prepare yourself some FULL ENGLISH or FULL AMERICAN, then you should try it out our variety too. I'd be willing to bet my life savings that the full English is NOT something every Englishman eats everyday, to be honest, what I described is much closer to what we eat everyday than only pão de queijo. 

But, alas, I don't think we would've won, that one from the Philippines, México, Turkey and Indian looked all very fire and that would beat our breakfast, but it would certainly not be the second most simple dish there outside of France's croissant and I think we'd get past English that's for sure.

Author: @remmy57
Content: I've had traditional breakfasts in several countries.  England and Ireland are quite similar and it really depends on the chef.  Both of these will be very welcoming to any real American man.  They feature key elements like eggs and sausage and toast.  They totally out-class the American versions simply because the ingredients haven't been corrupted by "big food".  The taste is like American food was back in the 60's and earlier.  However, I am originally from the Southwestern US and have a particular fondness for Chorizo (a sausage common in Mexican cuisine) and tortillas.  Notice the Irish and English breakfasts have baked beans.  The Mexican b/fast has refried beans (delicious).  How in the name of flavor did Mexican b/fast not make this list?   Americans are generally wanting eggs and either bacon or sausage and toast.  That is a proper American breakfast.  I you like cereal, don't even talk to me.  Please note:  not all cultures in EU have eggs at b/fast.  Germany does.  France usually has a croissant or fresh bakery bread with a hard crust, brie cheese and a cafe with cream (think latte or cappuccino).  Italy is usually an espresso/cappuccino and a pastry of any sort.  In Copenhagen, Denmark there was the SAS Falconer Center Hotel that had THE BEST breakfast buffet ever.  They had crepes, sausages, eggs, ham...you name it.  So, what's the best breakfast?  Answer: it's what you got in front of you when you're starving when you wake up.  Everything tastes awesome when you're really hungry!  Italy  has probably the best food overall but their breakfast is minimalist. I loved the dinners in India but never had a real breakfast there.  PS Canadian breakfast absolutely rocks!  I ate at this family diner owned by a Greek family on Young Street in Ontario.  The quality was something deserving of a "Diners, Drive-ins and Dives" TV show feature. Eggs, pancakes bacon, the works. 5 stars.

Content: The way I was cheering so hard for Philippines and it emerged as the winner!! I'm just happy that Filipino breakfast food or Filipino food in general is finally getting the recognition it deserves. Longsilog is just one of the staple breakfast meal here in the Philippines. There are other "silog" variants depending on what meat it's paired with. Silog is from two words- SInangag (garlic fried rice) + itLOG (egg). If you have bangus (a kind of fish), it will be called bangsilog. And there's also the famous tapsilog which is combination of the garlic fried rice + egg + tapa (cured beef similar to beef jerky). I really recommend it to people who haven't tried it :)

Author: @carlosandalucia4660
Content:
First, every nation loves their own breakfast. 
There is no other breakfast at second place for them, that belongs to other nations. 
So, these comparisons are just BS.

Second, neighboring countries have similar breakfast types, like UK and Irish.
So, there is no need to have two similar breakfasts to compete with each other.

Third, there are multiple alternatives for breakfast in each culture.
When you call Menemen is the Turkish breakfast, you generate an impression as if everyone in the country wakes up with Menemen, which is not the case at all. Menemen is just a dish that everyone loves and eats only once in a while, not every day. 
There are lot more preferences for breakfast that changes from person to person.
People who are working 8 to 5, people who are running their own stores, people who are students, housewives, retires, at vacation places and so on. There are easy and quick breakfasts, and there are buffet style extended breakfasts.
Each of those groups have different breakfast than the other, while individuals in the same group can also go with different preferences among themselves.
Every nation has their own bread types, baked goods, egg dishes, hot and cold drinks, cheeses / olives, dry meats, jams, honey,  dips and spreads, different sweets and so on.... Your comparisons are too short than the real breakfast options. That makes your ratings just BS.

Forth, you cannot compare a meat soup from Vietnam with an egg scramble from Turkey.
You may compare the egg dishes and two meat soups from two countries with each other, if you need to.
You must compare the dishes that are made with the same ingredients.

You selected Menemen as the second best, while Tunisia is proud of having shakshuka in their cuisine and probably claiming to be the owner of the original recipe. But, you did not even compare Tunisian breakfast with others at all. That is the 5th BS.

Let me know when you absorb all these. Then I can tell more.

Author: @LeftCatcher
Content:
Instead of an English breakfast, I make an American variant.
2 eggs over-easy as toad in the hole.
4 slices of traditional Jimmy Dean sausage (from the tube not that frozen crap).
 4 strips of smoked bacon well cooked but still bendable (no burnt bacon).
Home fries (fried cubes of potato diced to 6.35mm for the euro crowd).
And a small can of Bushes baked beans, liberally salted with kosher salt (flakey salt).
Served with dry white toast and coffee.

Cooking:
Bacon first to render the bacon fat.
With the bacon fat, add butter and fry up the home fries.
Then the sausage.
Then heat up your beans in a small sauce pot while cooking the eggs as toad in the whole over easy. (I want to make those "cheese uncrustables" with the bread centers you talked about in your egg video 🤤).
Plate it all up, top everything with beans, toast and coffee on the side.

Note: American baked beans are from a barbecue base sauce, not just ketchup, so it's sweet, mix that with salty, and a little Sriracha if your feeling adventurous (thought I tend to like it better without) and the flavors mix well.
But it is anything but traditional.
Bon appetit, you need it with a meal this big.

Content:
Brazilian breakfast is just COFFEE. Other things are optional and vary according to region. This is a very light meal for us, and many people just drink black coffee and go to work.

Coffee is very important, to the point that breakfast in PT-BR is "café da manhã", which means MORNING COFFEE. (But in PT-PT it is "pequeno almoço ")

Other than coffee I would say "pão na chapa", but I'm from São Paulo. It sure is regional. Our breakfasts are very light and simple, many people skip them, maybe they shouldn't even be in this competition.

I can see the strawberry jam is a substitution for guava jam (goiabada), but most people will eat pão de queijo by itself, with no additional ingredient.

Author: @ilikehardplay
Content:
While I agree that Philippine breakfasts are vastly underappreciated on the world stage, and worthy of a top ranking...

..I'd just argue that you didn't pick the BEST -silog breakfast.  The name of the dish is actually a portmanteau word for the three main ingredients that make up the dish:  The two staples of the dish are sinangag (garlic fried rice) and itlog (fried egg) ....making up the root of -silog.  The prefix to the various -silogs is the accompanying protein...  Thus what you tasted was longsilog...  the shortened form representing longganisa sausages.  But there is also Tapsilog, which is marinated fried beef (Tapa); Bangsilog, which included marinated fried milkfish (Bangus); Spamsilog....yes, with frried Spam for the protein; and my personal favorite, Tocilog, which includes marinated, fried pork that somewhat resembles Chinese red-cooked pork (Tocino)....which is just delightful as a breakfast combination.  Or you can go overboard to gluttonous joy with more than one of the proteins for a super silog.

Author: @NelPJ
Content: I don't know why the hell you think Brazilian breakfast is cheese bread (pão de queijo) and jam. What a gross error, the result of misinformation... I could say that even in the state of Minas Gerais, where pão de queijo is a kind of cultural landmark, they eat pão de queijo in the morning as a general daily habit. Perhaps the most popular breakfast in Brazil is coffee with milk, possibly a fruit juice, bread with butter (a variation of the French baguette), some kind of cheese or requeijão ( a kind of cream cheese), and fruit such as bananas or papaya. Tapioca and corn couscous are also very common in the North and Northeast regions, and have been rapidly adopted in other Brazilian states in the last decade. Pão de Queijo is a national pride, but is usually eaten in the middle of the afternoon with a cup of strong coffee. Some add butter, cream cheese, dulce de leche or, less commonly, jam. Big mistake by the video producer... It's absurd to compare a "Full English Breakfast" with a Brazilian snack that isn't even our traditional breakfast. Bad job, guys.

Author: @HolllyDemonX
Content:
The problem with discussing continental countries is that we are very likely to talk about foods that follow regional customs within the country itself.  
Due to the difference in climate here in Brazil, not all 27 states eat *pão de queijo* for breakfast, and I would even say that fewer than 10 states commonly consume *pão de queijo*.  
The most common breakfast here in Brazil will always include fruit juice or seasonal fruits according to the state, strong black coffee, some type of bread with butter, jam, or cream cheese, some type of cake (cornmeal, cassava, orange, or lime), and if there is no bread, tapioca is an alternative.

Author: @go-duran
Content:
As a Mexican, I was disappointed seeing my least favorite type of Chilaquiles in the ranking. In Mexico you can usually choose which kind of sauce you want, usually with the options for Green (tomatillo-based), Red (tomato-based, although sometimes it's the dried chile version you made), Tatemada (charred chile, onion and tomatillo and/or tomato base), Divorced (red on one half, green on the other), and someplaces you can even get Mole (savory chocolate base), which is also delicious. You usually also get a choice of toppings, like shredded chicken, eggs, cecina (a type of steak), and/or melted cheese, and they're always served with refried beans. My personal favorite is getting Divorciados so I can get more variety of flavors, or Tatemada, which has a deeper flavor profile. Flavors also vary depending on where you order it, so it being ubiquitous means you can taste a bunch of different Chilaquiles and not get tired of them.
That being sad, Longsilog and Menemen look amazing, and I would absolutely try them should I see them on a menu.

LONGSILOG SWEEP!!!! The great thing about the Filipino breakfast is that you can change the ulam/meat/viand, so you can have tapsilog (with tapa), longsilog, chicksilog (chicken), spamsilog (spam), hotsilog (hotdogs), bangsilog (bangus, a type of fish) and so on. It gives you lots of choices while still having that wonderful balance of the full meal. It's usually a fatty meat, but can be anything flavourful that you prefer like fried eggplant, bacon, corned beef, etc. Tocilog is also a popular; tocino is a sweet/caramelized meat that's popular here as well, and goes well with the vinegar and the garlic rice.

So I argue that pho isn't a breakfast food for the vietnamese but vietnamese ice coffee is.

Author: @omarmendezdel
Content:
As a Colombian, I want to say a few things: 

1. COLOMBIA, COLOMBIA, COLOMBIA!!!!!! In your face, France! Of course arepa and huevos pericos (which is the exact form this eggs are called) are better than the croissant. 
2. That arepa is missing butter. There are many types of arepa in Colombia, and the one used in this recipe most have butter. You spread it when the arepa is hot, so it can melt, like in pancakes. Perfection! I think that with the butter, we could've won a few more points.
3. I think a better option for Colombia would've been the Colombian tamal and it is as common as the arepa con huevos. Personally, my favorite is the valluno tamal (from the Valle del Cauca region), but the most common in the country is the tolimense tamal (from the Tolima region). Fun facts: The SILOG meal has many varieties including the Longsilog feautured here and they're all S Tier. Try one for yourself and you'll know what I'm talking about 😂. I'd go as far as to claim that the Tapsilog version is SS tier.

The Silog is actually a shortened version of the dish's name. For example, Longsilog stands for:
-LONGganisa (the pork dish)
-SInangag (fried rice)
-itLOG (EGG)

or 

Tapsilog 
TAPa (beef dish)
SInangag (fried rice)
itLOG (Egg)

And many more variations lol.

Making it years later, sometimes I will use a ham steak instead of bacon and maybe throw in a small piece of good steak.

So about India on your channel; nearly every time India has been featured on your channel, the food has mainly been from the southern regions of India, such as dosa-sambar today. Content:
Your pho broth was way too dark.  It should be very light in color.  And it's usually served with pickled garlic, lime wedges, sliced bird's eye chilis, several varieties of hot sauce, and often some bánh quay (a type of fluffy fried bread stick).  You add these elements to taste and dunk the fried bread in the broth.  You can't really properly evaluate pho without those.

And, for the record, pho is hands down the best hangover food in the world, which is probably part of why it's such a popular breakfast food here as heavy drinking is the norm in Vietnam.

Content:

Author: @btkocc
Content: A Turkish breakfast almost always includes some other accoutrements alongside a main dish, in this case Menemen. There would be some sort of cured meat- like Sucuk or Pastırma, there would be different cheeses- usually Süzme Beyaz and Tulum, there would be different olives- like cured black olives and grilled green olives, there would be jams such as fig and strawberry, and veggies like cucumber and tomato with olive oil, of course all alongside Turkish black tea. This all seems high-effort but we almost always have all of these ingredients in our fridges, so it's just a matter of brewing some tea, making the menemen and putting all else on the table. Josh talks about how the menemen can get boring texturally and flavor-wise, which I agree with, and the accoutrements are the key to battling that. So, I do believe if put up against the Philippines Longsilog in its full glory, the Turkish breakfast would absolutely crush this competition.

Content:
Josh, as someone who’s married to a Turk, please try Van kahvaltisi (breakfast from Van, a city in Turkey).

As other commenters have already mentioned, menemen is a small component of Turkish breakfast, like serving the eggs only of an English breakfast. Bal kaymak (honey and clotted cream), variety of cheeses, olives, sucuk (garlic beef sausage), burek, boyoz (from İzmir region), tahin pekmez (sesame paste with molasses)….all with black tea on the side; I’m all for American breakfast (I’m Canadian) but Turks are a whole other breakfast level.

Author: @EricMcLovin13
Content:
Pão de Queijo is extremely versatile. while it's delicious on its own, you can pretty much do anything with it and still taste good. you can go simple and just spread butter or cream cheese inside it,  go for sweet flavours like doce de leite, chocolate, the guava jam you used, use meats, like sausages, bacon, ham, chicken, and even add more cheese onto it, as it's usually made with mozzarela and parmesan, you can go all out with more cheeses, like cheddar, canastra(if you guys have the chance, buy this one, it's deemed the best cheese we have, and it constantly figures in the world's best lists), reino which is my personal favourite, made on the region i live, it's dry, strong and somewhat spicy, and it was actually invented in my hometown, but sadly our growth stopped almost a century ago and we're currently losing population to other places(when i was born, we had 60k, right now we have 40k, most of my friends moved out, i lived elsewhere for a few years as well) which means there's no tech or investment for us to make the best in the country again


i lived through college eating lots of pão de queijo with sausage and bacon fillings, that we used to buy frozen in the market(it's been a few years since i saw it, which is sad, can only assume they broke) and there's so much potential with what you can do, that despite the fillings, me and my housemates would always invent something, which was the munchies talking



just beware if you're not from here and either plan to cook some or buy them in a cafe or any place that sells brazilian food, cause they're easy to do and even easier to mess up, and that almost always means they're dry as chalk if you use too much polvilho(cassava starch)



bon appetit my fellas, a big hug from a proud mineiro and please EAT OUR FOOD, you'll lose your mind with it

Content:
Giving more context about pão de queijo ( based on my everyday life ):

here in brazil, we prioritize eating less during breakfest to make room for Lunch ( compared with other countries ), and pão de queijo fits in this bill because of that ( and we eat a lot of bread too, since most our snacks comes from bread ). heck even mc donalds around here sell this with coffee as a breakfest combo ( but it cannot compete with proper bakery pão de queijo. )

and the coffee, yeah i agree most people don't like it ( which i have encontered some around my neighborhood, but it is strange for me since here is the land of coffee [ i live in são paulo, but people around here says the minas gerais version is better ] ), but this can be changed to a Orange juice or a Hot Chocolate, so that's not a issue.

and as a bonus, it fits well as afternoon snacks too ( i love to buy 5 -8 pães de queijo to eat with tea / coffee / hot chocolate / soda during the afternoon ) so... yeah pão de queijo is customizable depending of the place you live around here and your lifestyle.

In India, we have Breakfast for every state...

Kashmir have Porathe with Halwa and Kahwa
Punjab have Amritsari Kulcha with Lassi or Aloo Parantha with Lassi
UK have Aloo ke Gutke
Delhi have Choley Bhature
Gujarat have Dhokla, Fafda and Jalebi
Maharashtra have Poha, Vada Pav and Missal Pav
Indore have Poha with Jalebi while Itarsi have Poori Aloo
South have their Parotta Curry, Masala Dosa, Idli Sambar
North-East have separate variety. 

So! Pick any and you have a different flavour bomb.

Author: @kleervoyans
Content: Fun fact: Menemen does not have a single set recipe; it has multiple variations depending on the region in Turkey. The Aegean region has a different recipe, Central Anatolia has another, and so on. There is even a long-standing debate among Turkish people, as old as time, about whether Menemen should be cooked with or without onions and with or without sucuk. According to my taste, Menemen with onions and sucuk produces the best results. However, given that you cooked it without onions and used a rather large amount of eggs, and it still made the finals, shows just how delicious and versatile a breakfast dish Menemen is. Congrats to Phillipines, a worthy opponent!
